Natal long-fingered bat females give birth to a single offspring per year, a reproductive strategy that reflects the energetic constraints of a relatively small body size. Each female produces exactly one pup per litter [N_R_i = one pup per litter] and raises only a single litter annually [F_R_i = single litter annually], resulting in a low annual reproductive output typical of many cave-roosting insectivorous bats. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active roosting environment (35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]), the gestation period extends for approximately 150 days [tg = approximately 150 days], a duration that aligns with values reported for the closely related congener Miniopterus schreibersii. This lengthy pregnancy, combined with the production of a single precocial pup, suggests a life history pattern that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity, likely an adaptation to the unpredictable insect prey availability that characterizes their southern African habitats. Field records indicate that females terminate the single pregnancy in early summer, timing parturition to coincide with peak insect abundance.

Newborn pups of this species are exceptionally small, with a neonatal wet weight at birth of just 2.8 grams [Wwb = 2.8 grams]. This modest mass is comparable to that of other small vespertilionid bats and represents a relatively low investment per offspring compared to the ultimate adult body mass attained by females. The process of weaning, during which the pup transitions from exclusive reliance on maternal milk to independent foraging, occurs at 66 days after birth [tx = 66 days after birth] under the same roosting temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This relatively extended period of postnatal care is typical among insectivorous bats, which must teach their young to navigate the complex acoustic environment of echolocation. Maternal investment is therefore substantial during the first two months of life, a time during which the pup must also develop the flight muscles and sensory capabilities necessary for successful predation. The weaning age is thus a critical life-history transition, after which the young bat begins to face the challenges of independent foraging.

Adult female Natal long-fingered bats reach a typical ultimate body mass of approximately 12 grams [Wwi = approximately 12 grams], though published records indicate a range of 9 to 13 grams depending on reproductive status and season. This species is thus a member of the small-bodied bat guild, a trait that influences many aspects of its physiology and life history. Measurements of basal metabolism conducted during the active phase at a roost temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] reveal a resting oxygen consumption of 4.89 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 4.89 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value is consistent with the relatively high mass-specific metabolic rates expected for small insectivorous mammals and reflects the energetic demands of maintaining homeothermy at the elevated temperatures typical of maternity roosts. The species' elevated metabolic rate is supported by a diet of aerial insects captured during nocturnal foraging bouts, which are energetically costly but necessary to sustain both the female and her developing young.

Puberty in this species is attained at an age of 577 days after birth [tp = 577 days after birth], but crucially, this milestone is documented to occur at a higher body temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C], a condition associated with the active, flight-intensive phase of the adult bat. This thermal dependence suggests that the onset of gonadal maturation may be linked to the sustained elevation of core body temperature that accompanies flight activity, rather than being a purely age-dependent process. The comparatively late attainment of sexual maturity, nearly 1.6 years after birth, is a notable feature of this species' life history and aligns with the patterns observed in other cave-roosting miniopterids. This delay likely reflects the time required for juveniles to accumulate sufficient body reserves and foraging experience to successfully rear their own offspring. Reproductive maturity is therefore not simply a function of chronological age but is also influenced by thermoregulatory and metabolic factors that integrate with the species' distinctive roosting ecology.

Maximum recorded lifespan estimates for the Natal long-fingered bat, based on longitudinal studies of banded individuals and data from the congener Miniopterus schreibersii, reach as high as 22 years [am = 22 years] under natural cave-roosting conditions at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This exceptional longevity is remarkable for a mammal of only 12 grams body mass and places the species among the longest-lived small mammals known. Such extended lifespans are typically associated with slow life histories, low annual fecundity (with females producing a single pup each year), and the relatively low extrinsic mortality rates afforded by predator-protected cave habitats. The combination of delayed sexual maturation, prolonged lifespan, and low reproductive output suggests a bet-hedging strategy in which adults survive across multiple breeding seasons, maximizing lifetime reproductive success despite the constraints of an unpredictable prey base. This pattern reinforces the view of Miniopterus natalensis as a 'slow' life-history strategist among bats.
